subject: pufferfish
pitch: A startled pufferfish fully puffed up into a ball. Creamy yellow skin with brown leopard spots on top fading to a white belly, short spikes all over, a tiny pouting mouth, big worried round eyes, small fluttering side fins and a stubby fan-shaped tail. A few bubbles rise from its mouth.
reasoning:
I'm planning a puffed pufferfish design facing +Z, considering how it should float or rest with its lowest points touching y=0 without anything hanging below the ground plane.

I'll go with a body radius around 0.17m for a stylized puffed porcupinefish, with belly spikes defining the lowest contact points. For the skeleton, I'm sketching a spine chain running from snout to tail through the body center, plus joints for head, jaw, pectoral fins, and eyes, with the body shape approximated as a sphere-like sweep along that spine.

Defining the radius function...

A lathe revolve would give a clean faceted sphere profile, but I think the skeleton-first approach calls for a proper spine chain instead, so I'll set up a sweep across a 3-joint spine that lets the body bend naturally.

I'm placing a root joint at the hips and building the spine chain outward from there, running the path from tail toward the head so it reads as a natural forward-facing rig.

The tail extends beyond the ball as a peduncle then fans out, with its own separate sweep from the body. I'm calculating the exact spike geometry — using cone height and embed depth to figure out how far the spikes protrude from the body surface, which determines the center height placement to keep the lowest spike tip properly positioned.

I'll accept a tiny 2% sink and set cy=0.2, keeping the tip just slightly below zero, which is acceptable. I also need to double check the tube's bottom radius at the midpoint sample matches the ring sampling so the surface aligns correctly.

Since this is a floating fish, I don't need it resting on anything, so I'll just add rising bubbles near the mouth, positioning them above and in front of the fish rather than beneath it.

Actually a textured card would disappear edge-on, so I'll skip that and go simpler: solid low-poly icosahedron spheres in pale cyan with a small white highlight patch to suggest bubble shine, keeping things readable in a stylized low-poly style.

Now for the body: a cream-yellow base with brown leopard rosette spots on top, fading into a white belly via a countershading paint that blends based on surface normal, with a soft parameter to widen the transition so spots naturally vanish toward the belly.

Nesting a countershade into white on top of the spotted body could work, but then the spots themselves won't fade properly. Better to nest the fade into the spot color itself, so spots blend toward yellow before the overall body countershades into white near the belly.

For the spikes, I'm considering whether they should reuse the body's paint for positional consistency, or get a custom gradient so the tips read as a darker brown against the yellow base.

Running the numbers, spike surface area is comparable to body surface area, but texel density still works out to roughly 0.9mm per texel, which is plenty fine resolution. I'm also considering just using flat colors for spikes to simplify things.

Since flat colors count against the 64-color limit, I'll stick with the position-based paint gradient for spikes rather than adding more distinct colors—likely reusing the same skin paint. For placement, I'm thinking of scattering spikes across the body surface using a minimum-distance constraint, with the count determined by the ~0.34 m² surface area and a spacing of roughly 0.045m between spikes.

Spikes need to avoid clustering near the eyes, mouth, fins, and tail base, so I'll filter scattered points by distance from those feature positions. For geometry, I'm picturing short low-poly cones, around 0.011m base radius and 0.04-0.045m length, with flat shading to keep them crisp and spiky-looking.

For orientation, each cone's local +Y tip aligns to the surface normal at that point, with a default embed depth of about 0.2. I'll vary their scale slightly between 0.75 and 1.0, keeping the geometry calculations such that no spike tip pokes below the body's lowest point.

For the eyes, I'm going for big round worried eyes with white sphere eyeballs, small pupils for a startled look, and small slanted brow-ridge wedges whose inner ends sit higher to convey worry. I'm placing the eyes at roughly ±55° azimuth and 20° elevation so they read well from the front, with a radius around 0.05 to make them appropriately large.

Decals could work for projecting texture onto the eyeball sphere, but I think stuck parts give a more primitive, tactile 3D look -- so I'll build the iris as a stuck flattened cylinder shape instead of a flat texture.

Working through the eye geometry: sclera as a small cream-white sphere, with the iris as a short cylinder disk raised on its surface. I'm checking how much the disk edge would sink into the curved sclera surface versus how much it needs to protrude to stay visible.

Thinking about an alternative: using a spherical cap for the iris instead, sized slightly larger than the eye sphere and cut to a polar angle so it naturally conforms to the curvature without the edge disappearing.

I'll go with placing the bottom of the bounding box at the surface minus embed*height, so resizing doesn't require retuning — a cone of height h would have its base at surface-0.2h and tip at surface+0.8h, matching my earlier assumption. For the sphere cap, I need the bbox min y value.

Checking the geometry more carefully: a cap seated this way just sits on the sclera surface as a disc, which creates the same clipping issue as the cylinder — the rim of the cap dips below the curved sphere surface unless I use a larger embed value to sink it in, so the visible cap only shows where its height exceeds the sphere's local drop.

Let me try a cleaner approach instead — placing an iris ellipsoid directly along the eye's gaze direction relative to the eye center, computing how far it needs to sit outward so it clears the sclera surface at both the center and edges without clipping.

Still working on the flattening logic...

For the eyes themselves, I'll build them as layered 3D shapes with a small white highlight sphere for shine, plus worried-looking brows above them. Thinking about placement: on a pufferfish the eyes sit on the sides of the head, so I'll position them symmetrically around the body surface at an outward angle, slightly embedded so they read as part of the form.

I want eye joints so the eyes can rotate independently, created as children of the head joint with gaze direction set along their aim. Now I'm moving on to the mouth -- a small puckered, beak-like pout positioned at the front of the body, with separate upper and lower jaw parts attached to a jaw joint near the head.

For the pouting "o" shape, I'm thinking I could lathe a small ring profile around the z-axis, like a fat donut cross-section, giving an outer radius around 0.03 and inner radius around 0.012, with a dark disc filling the inside to suggest the mouth opening.

To let the mouth open, I realize I need separate upper and lower halves instead of one full ring — using half-torus arcs (0 to π for the upper lip, rotated by π for the lower lip) so each jaw piece can move independently while still joining at the mouth corners.

The lower lip parents to a jaw bone with a hinge pivot near the back of the mouth, while a dark cylinder sits just inside the ring to suggest the oral cavity, plus small white boxes for upper and lower teeth.

I need to account for the sphere's curvature near the mouth opening — the surface recedes slightly there, so I'm calculating the actual z-depth at the mouth's position to place the lip ring just outside that curved surface, offset by the tube radius for a slight protrusion.

For puffiness, I'm adding a flattened, scaled sphere beneath the ring as a muzzle bulge, painted in a cream tone using position-based skin paint so it blends seamlessly. I'm skipping extra details like rosy cheek blush since it's not essential to the design, and setting the mouth's vertical position below center to match a typical low fish-mouth placement.

Working out eye placement, I'm computing the direction vector from spherical coordinates with azimuth around 50° and elevation 20°, giving eye centers roughly at x=±0.12, protruding with radius 0.055 so they're visible from the front. For gaze direction I'm tilting slightly more forward (azimuth ~42°, elevation ~12°) so the pupils read as looking toward the viewer for that startled expression, and now I'm thinking through how to shape worried brows as curved body-colored eyelid caps over the upper portion of each eye, slanted so the inner side sits higher.

Reworking it: with the axis tilted outward-and-up instead, moving inward along the edge plane rises — that gives the inner end higher than the outer, matching the worried-brow slant I want. So the lid cap's pole points up-and-outward, meaning it covers more of the eye's outer-upper region.

Setting up the local coordinate math now rather than relying on lookAt, so I can place eye parts correctly relative to the gaze direction.

Still computing lid orientation basis...

Working through the cross product to get the outer sideways vector perpendicular to both gaze and eye-up, checking the sign convention so the outer direction points away from the face center for each side.

Now I'm setting up the lid axis as a combination of the lateral and outward vectors rotated by 25 degrees, and figuring out the lid cap's angular radius and placement relative to the gaze direction so the eyelid appears positioned correctly on the eyeball surface.

Thinking through the geometry, I realize the lid shouldn't cover the iris for a startled expression — that look needs full white visible around the iris, with worry conveyed through the brow instead. So I'm shrinking the iris's angular radius to about 30 degrees and recalculating the lid edge to sit around 45 degrees from the gaze direction.

Viewed from the eye's gaze direction, the lid appears as a convex arc bulging toward the a-direction, with its lowest point at that outward tilt, which explains the slanted brow-like appearance in projection.

That confirms the slant direction works with the inner edge rising. For color, I'll paint the lid using the skin tone since it sits atop the sclera as a thin shell, and I'm considering adding a subtle dark brown rim along the lid edge to suggest a lash line.

Rather than a rim, I think a simple chunky brown eyebrow shape above each eye, angled with the inner point higher than the outer, would read more clearly as "worried" while staying cartoonish -- even though real pufferfish lack brows, this stylization works well with the lid approach for a cute, expressive look.

Wait, there's a gap problem: since the lid cap radius (0.062) exceeds the sclera radius (0.055), the rim floats above the sclera surface with a visible gap at the edge where you'd see inside the eye. To fix this hollow look, I should match the lid edge more closely to the sclera, maybe by adjusting the cap radius or adding an inner bevel.

For colors, I'll go with an amber iris, dark pupil, and white highlights to give a startled expression—keeping the pupil small relative to a larger iris, with two highlights of different sizes for a more dynamic look.

Now I'm thinking through the pectoral fins: small fan-shaped fins extending from the sides, built with an extruded outline and attached via a joint. I'm debating what role to assign the fin joint in the skeleton system, since fins don't map cleanly to existing categories like arm or wing.

Writing fin ray pattern paint...

For placement, I'll position the pectoral fin behind the eye at roughly 105° azimuth and -5° elevation, angled outward and back about 40° from the body surface.

The fin shape is a narrow-based fan spreading to a rounded paddle, like a pufferfish's pectoral fin held roughly vertical but angled slightly away from the body, extending outward and backward from its base point.

With that direction the fin faces mostly front-on to the viewer, which works well. I'm defining the fin outline as a small fan shape with a narrow root widening to a rounded tip, smoothed, and sinking the root slightly into the body so it reads as attached rather than floating.

For a natural resting pose I'm giving the fins a slight upward tilt rather than keeping them perfectly flat, while staying symmetric left-to-right, then setting up a simple hinge joint at the fin base with a short three-joint chain running along the fin's centerline so it can be rigged like a small limb.

I'm reconsidering the fin structure though — rather than one rigid extrude per fin, I could use a membrane stretched between a leading-edge chain and a trailing-edge chain, which would let the fin bend smoothly across its surface instead of staying stiff.

I'm working out the chain-naming convention: a path's joint count follows span count between points, so with 3 points (root, mid, tip) I'd need matching names to get root and tip joints correctly labeled.

Now shifting to the tail: it's a short tapered peduncle narrowing from the ball's rear, leading into a fan-shaped tail fin extruded vertically in the Y-Z plane with thickness along X.

Checking the fan-shaped polygon points to confirm the outline traces a non-self-intersecting path from root around the scalloped edge and back, with smoothing applied to round the corners.

For the tail coloring, I'm using radial angle and distance from the fin origin to create a cream-yellow base with darker rays and a brown outer margin band, matching a dogface pufferfish look. Then I'm setting up the tail joint chain as a backward sequence of named points (tail1, tail2, tail3) extending from the hip root toward the fin tip.

Working out exact z-coordinates for the peduncle and fan sections, I'm trying to keep total fish length proportional even though it's longer than a real pufferfish's stubby body—deciding to shrink the peduncle and fan segments to around 0.165 to 0.30 in z to keep things compact.

Since the ball is nearly rigid, joint bending won't really matter for the skin smoothness. I could simplify by sweeping the body as a straight two-point path from z=-0.175 to z=+0.175, with bone assignments for tail, hips, and front chain segments.

Actually, binding the whole body rigidly to just the hips joint might be more robust — simpler sphere shape, fewer weird skinning artifacts — while the spine chain (hips → spine1 → spine2 → head) handles just the head, jaw, and eyes. That tradeoff feels safer than smooth-skinning across multiple spine bones, which risks distortion.

I'm building a catmull-rom path for the body from a handful of points, then finding where the hips joint sits along it to split the path into a front "spine" chain and a back "tail" chain, both parented to hips. I want the tail chain to extend further out, so I'm adjusting the body shape accordingly.

For the tail specifically, I'm constructing a separate extended catmull path starting at hips and reaching further back, since the sweep only cares about the projection onto the path rather than requiring an exact slice match -- confirming this is valid since each joint just owns the segment where it projects. Now I'm working through how the sweep bone list (tail, hips, front) applies radii along that separate tail path starting from the hips center.

The fan should attach to tail4, the last joint in the chain, with role 'tail'. Now I'm moving to the front chain, laying out a path from the hips toward the head.

For this I'll use spine1 and spine2 as the span joints, then a separate "head" joint anchored off spine2 aimed along the forward tangent, with a "jaw" joint parented to head at the mouth hinge point.

Now I'm working out the body's radius profile along its length, using a parametric curve to taper the cross-section from a sphere-like center outward, with slight asymmetry between width and height for a more natural shape.

I'll set sides to 14, giving an even count with a flat bottom face, and figure that with roughly 14 rings the sphere faceting will be visible but acceptable for a low-poly look. I'm also weighing whether to abandon the sweep approach entirely in favor of a lathe operation instead.

For the sweep itself, a radius function tapering to 0.012 with round caps should work fine, and since the path runs straight along z, the rings will just circle normally using transported frame defaults—I'll rely on position-based painting rather than sector angles. For spots and countershading I'll use position and surface normal respectively, and for eye placement I need to query the surface around an explicit center point like [0, CY, 0] rather than trusting the default bounding box center. Now I need to work out how the head joint attaches and how other items get stuck onto the body via hit queries.

Each spike inherits blended bone weights from its hit point on the skinned mesh, so they'll bend naturally with the skin rather than staying rigid—that's acceptable even with the overhead across roughly 150 separate spike parts, since I'm well within the 1000-part limit. Tallying everything up: body plus ~140 spikes, ~14 eye parts, ~8 mouth parts, fins, tail, and bubbles gets me to around 190 parts total, and triangle counts are trivial (cones with 5-6 radial segments give maybe 10 tris each), so there's plenty of budget left to add more spikes or finer detail.

I'm scattering spikes across the sphere surface with a minimum-distance constraint, estimating that random sequential placement will saturate around 190 points even though I'm requesting 240—should be close enough. I'm varying spike scale slightly for a more organic look and considering whether to add darker tips via custom UV-based paint on the cone geometry, checking how three.js maps v-coordinates from base to tip to get that gradient right.

Adding spike tip coloring logic...

Since textures get downscaled when they don't fit, maybe it's safer to just give spikes flat color instead of painted texture, freeing up sheet space — using two cream tones for top and bottom.

To avoid a visible step in color at the ball's spike edges, I'm thinking of mapping spike color to hit position with a five-step palette based on the normal's y-value, picking from a small set of golden-to-cream tones so it still reads as a smooth gradient while keeping the color count low.

Two-toning each spike tip would need extra geometry, so I'm setting that aside as not worth the complexity. Checking UV space instead, I calculate the surface area from the 240 spikes plus the body and other parts comes to roughly 0.9 m², which at the target texel density fits comfortably within a 1024x1024-ish texture even with gutters, so the atlas layout isn't a concern.

Now I'm deciding on the body's skin pattern: brown rosette-style leopard spots versus plain blotchy spots. I'll go with rosette-ringed spots in dark brown for that classic leopard look, trusting the ring rendering will hold up at this texel resolution rather than looking noisy.

For the mouth, I'm computing the surface hit point from the center direction with a slight downward tilt (azimuth 0, elevation -12°), using the sweep cross-section to find the actual position on the ball. Then I place a small skin-colored muzzle bump there using a scaled sphere to create a subtle protruding mouth shape.

I'm then placing a small dark disc cylinder just behind the lip opening to simulate the dark interior of the pout, sizing it to match the torus hole so it reads as the mouth cavity rather than a visible gap.

For teeth, I'm adding two thin white boxes near the top and bottom of the opening to suggest tiny buck teeth, but with the hole only about 18mm across I'm reconsidering the ring radius so the teeth are actually visible rather than hidden inside the torus tube.

For lip color, I'm leaning toward a warm salmon-pink like "#ee9a78" to give the pufferfish a cute pouty mouth that pops against the creamy yellow body, rather than matching the skin tone exactly. I'm also structuring the bone hierarchy so the upper lip, muzzle, and upper tooth attach to the head while the lower lip and tooth attach to the jaw, and sketching how the half-torus arc should sweep from the right side up through the top to form the upper lip shape.

For the lower lip I need to flip that arc by baking a 180-degree rotation directly into the geometry rather than relying on orientation parameters, since torus half-shapes are tricky to orient reliably through the dir/axis system. I'm also working out where to place the jaw hinge joint — it needs to sit behind the lower lip so the jaw bone aims forward toward the mouth center, letting the jaw rotate open naturally around that pivot.

Now I'm mapping out the spine chain: hips at the root, then spine1 and spine2 spans up to about z=0.16, with a head joint branching off spine2 aimed forward, and the jaw joint attached near the mouth hinge. I'm computing the eye center by taking the surface hit's position and nudging it slightly inward along the normal, and determining the gaze direction as a vector pointing toward a slightly different azimuth/elevation than the eye's own placement so the eyes bulge forward near the normal. Working through the actual numeric coordinates now to get the eye center position in Cartesian space.

Checking the eye's radius against the body silhouette at that depth confirms the eyes bulge outward noticeably while still leaving a reasonable gap between them, giving a wide-eyed, worried look with visible protrusion once I account for the sunken sclera depth. Checking whether the lid covers the iris: given the iris sits at about 32-33° from the gaze direction and the lid edge falls near 40° from gaze, the iris stays just clear of the lid, leaving enough visible sclera around it for a believable eye.
